=== Step ingest-throughput: scripts/bench/ingest-throughput.sh ===
[main] INFO org.ulpgc.tarantino.bench.manifest.ManifestTool - Started run 20261105-215351-ingest-throughput-c1376c7 in benchmarks\runs\20261105-215351-ingest-throughput-c1376c7\manifest.json
Machine: the official one, with 24 hardware threads, 8 fast P cores and 16 slower E cores, without hyperthreading
Premise: ingestion is bound by the crawlers' CPU, not by Mongo. In the preliminary run the crawlers used 400-790 % CPU and Mongo about 100 %, and JFR put over half of the crawler samples in GutenbergText.bookText
Series replicas: 1, 2 and 3 crawler replicas with 8 workers each
H1: throughput grows with replicas but less than linearly: 8 workers fit in the 8 P cores, while 16 and 24 spill onto the slower E cores, so the gain from 2 to 3 replicas is smaller than from 1 to 2
Series workers: 4, 8 and 16 workers in 1 crawler replica
H2: throughput grows from 4 to 8 workers, which still fit in the P cores, and flattens towards 16, whose extra workers run on the E cores
Time windows: the whole one, from the first download claim to the last book downloaded, is the main figure; the steady one, between the downloads that complete 10 % and 90 % of the books, shows how much start-up and tail weigh

[main] INFO org.ulpgc.tarantino.bench.manifest.ManifestTool - Started run 20261105-220915-index-throughput-c1376c7 in benchmarks\runs\20261105-220915-index-throughput-c1376c7\manifest.json
Opened run 20261105-220915-index-throughput-c1376c7: candidates mirror, replicas 1 2 3, 5 repetitions, phases up to 1800 s
Machine: the official one, 24 hardware threads, 8 P cores and 16 E cores; each indexer replica indexes one batch at a time on its index-batches thread, so at most 3 indexing threads run and they fit in the P cores
Factors: books per batch and indexer replicas, 5 repetitions each, interleaved: repetition 1 of every configuration, then repetition 2, so drift over the run spreads across every configuration
Trial: the corpus is ingested once; each trial recreates the indexers with its configuration and rebuilds the index into a new generation
Window: the whole one only, from the first index claim to the last batch published in the trial's generation; it leaves out the up to 30 s control takes to reindex the books and to switch generation
Batch timeout: 2 s, so the last partial batch of each replica does not wait 30 s inside the window
Series batch: 1, 10, 100 and 250 books per batch with 1 indexer replica
H1: books per second rise from 1 to 100 books per batch and flatten from 100 to 250, because each batch pays a fixed cost (its lease, the postings bulkWrites, publishing and marking) that more books share, while tokenizing and writing postings cost the same per book
Series replicas: 1, 2 and 3 indexer replicas with batches of 100
H2: books per second grow with replicas but less than linearly: three indexing threads do not run out of CPU, and every replica writes its postings to the same Mongo, which becomes the bottleneck
H3: batches of 250 fit in -Xmx512m without OutOfMemoryError, but the indexer's memory in stats.csv peaks higher than with batches of 100, because a batch keeps the term frequencies and postings of all its books until it writes them

[main] INFO org.ulpgc.tarantino.bench.manifest.ManifestTool - Started run 20261105-235758-resource-usage-c1376c7 in benchmarks\runs\20261105-235758-resource-usage-c1376c7\manifest.json
Opened run 20261105-235758-resource-usage-c1376c7: candidates mirror, replicas 1 2 3, 5 repetitions, phases up to 1800 s
Factor: replicas of crawler and indexer together (1 2 3), 5 repetitions each, interleaved: repetition 1 of every N, then repetition 2, so drift over the run spreads across every N
Phases: ingestion with no indexer until every book is DOWNLOADED, then indexing with the indexers until every book is PUBLISHED
H1: during ingestion the total CPU of the crawlers grows with N while the CPU per crawler stays flat, until the 24 hardware threads of the official machine saturate
H2: during ingestion the crawlers use far more CPU than Mongo, as in the preliminary ingest-throughput run (crawlers 400-790 %, Mongo about 100 %), because the crawler spends its CPU processing the text
H3: during indexing Mongo takes a larger share of the CPU than during ingestion, and it grows with N, because every indexer writes its postings to the same Mongo
H4: the memory of each JVM stays flat below its -Xmx512m whatever N is

Machine: the official one, 24 hardware threads, 8 P cores and 16 E cores
Factors: coordination mode (hazelcast activemq activemq-persistent polling orchestrator) and replicas of crawler and indexer together (1 2 3), 5 repetitions each, interleaved: the 15 configurations of repetition 1, then repetition 2, so drift spreads across every mode
H0: download_ms does not differ between any pair of modes, nor indexing_ms between any pair without polling (differs false in pairs.csv), so only the coordination changed
H0 in polling: a batch claims each book as it polls it, so the wait for the batch to fill counts in indexing_ms instead of index_queue_wait; their sum compares through time_to_publication
polling H1: throughput within the CI of hazelcast, since the work per book dominates
polling H2: MongoDB CPU higher than in hazelcast at every N: one sorted findOneAndUpdate per claim, plus the idle polls
polling H3: publication visibility median about 2.5 s
activemq H1: throughput and time to publication within the CI of hazelcast at every N
activemq-persistent H2: throughput within the CI of activemq, with more broker CPU
orchestrator H1: throughput within the CI of hazelcast at N = 1 and 2; at N = 3 it may fall below, because one thread sends one POST at a time
orchestrator H2: time to publication up to two ticks (400 ms) above hazelcast
orchestrator H3: publication visibility under 300 ms
